speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: There was an outpouring of sympathy from Singaporeans all across the island on CFC(NS) Pang's passing as we shared the grief of the family's tragic loss.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I pray that the passage of time will bring some comfort to the Pang family as well as to the other families affected by the recent deaths of National Servicemen.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Your questions today as Members of Parliament (MPs) are an important part of holding the Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) and the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) accountable for the safety of our Servicemen and will strengthen our collective resolve to make SAF training as safe as possible and prevent such tragic deaths from occurring again.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: My Statement today will cover three areas: first, the death of CFC(NS) Aloysius Pang; second, the Committee of Inquiry (COI) findings of CFC Liu Kai; and third, safety enhancements by the SAF following recent National Service (NS) training deaths.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They comprise the chairperson who is a judge nominated by the State Courts, a consultant medical specialist, a member nominated by the External Review Panel on SAF Safety (ERPSS), a member of the Workplace Safety and Health Council (WSHC) and a senior-ranked national serviceman.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The COI has started its investigation to determine the circumstances and contributory factors which led to the demise of CFC(NS) Pang.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: When completed, the COI will submit its findings to the AFC and ERPSS.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Based on SIB's investigations, the Chief Military Prosecutor will decide if any servicemen are to be prosecuted for criminal or military offences in a Military Court.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Military Court is presided over by the State Court judges appointed as Presidents of the General Court Martial.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In this Statement, I will give as much information as possible without prejudicing the COI and SIB's investigations, whose findings, in due course, will be authoritative and conclusive.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: To preserve the integrity of the process, I will only state facts in reply to Parliamentary Questions (PQs) and consciously not draw any inferences or conclusions on the incident involving CFC(NS) Pang.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I ask Members here to observe the same.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We should also be mindful of the need to be sensitive to the family's feelings as we honour the memory of CFC(NS) Pang.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: On 19 January this year, three SAF personnel were in the cabin of the Singapore Self-Propelled Howitzer (SSPH) to carry out repair works on the gun's calibration system for accurate firing.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The three SAF personnel were CFC(NS) Pang, a Regular Armament Technician holding the rank of Military Expert (ME)2 with more than 16 years in service, and third, the Gun Detachment Commander, who is a Third Sergeant NSman.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Can I ask for the first slide to be displayed?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That gives Members the dimensions of the cabin within.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The gun barrel, which, on the left-hand side of the screen, is now in the inclined position and, therefore, is lowered in the rear, divides the cabin into two.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There is space for the three persons within the cabin to occupy positions on either side of the gun as shown in the diagram – 1, 2 and 3, and looking towards the SSPH from the back, about 1.55 metres on the left side, Safe Position 1 and 2; and 0.9 metres in width on the right side, Safe Position 3.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These so-called Safe Positions are designed to be occupied by the gun commander, the ammo loader and charge loaders, but for the purpose of the Statement, I will refer to them as "safe positions".

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The gun barrel is usually tilted upwards for firing, that is, the picture shown on the top, smaller picture on the left; the gun barrel at the inclined position with the gun pointed up.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The gun barrel is usually tilted upwards for firing but needs to be lowered for some types of maintenance work.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I will have some more pictures to make it clearer later.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Because of this, no one should be behind the barrel when the gun is being lowered.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: After he sustained these injuries, CFC(NS) Pang was treated onsite by the SAF Medical Officer and evacuated to Waiouru Camp Medical Centre.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: He was heli-evacuated to Waikato hospital in Hamilton, New Zealand, which is a regional trauma centre, where surgeons decided that he needed an operation to treat his injuries.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Prior to his first surgery, CFC(NS) Pang was conscious and speaking.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: At the first operation, the surgical team found that a number of organs were damaged and treated them accordingly.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: After the first surgery, CFC(NS) Pang did not require any ventilation and his vital signs were stable.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In fact, after the first surgery, he spoke with his mother who had been flown over to New Zealand.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: A "second-look" surgery had been planned for CFC(NS) Pang on 21 January 2019, two days after the first surgery.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: According to the surgeons there, this was to detect further injuries, as damage from compression injuries may only show up later.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: No further damage was discovered at the second-look surgery, but despite this, CFC(NS) Pang's condition subsequently deteriorated.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I propose now to deal with Members' questions which fall in three broad categories: first, what was the experience and state of the maintenance crew?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: CFC(NS) Pang had arrived in New Zealand on 6 January 2019 and had begun maintenance work from 10 January 2019.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, on 6 January, he arrived; he began maintenance work on 10 January.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This was CFC(NS) Pang’s seventh In-Camp Training (ICT).

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: He had been trained to perform maintenance and repair for the SSPH since he was a full-time national serviceman (NSF).

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In addition, during his previous ICT in February 2018, he had attended a two-day refresher Maintenance Vocation Training on the basic functional checks and troubleshooting for the SSPH.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That course also included safety procedures during gun movements.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Before participating in Exercise Thunder Warrior this year, CFC(NS) Pang had undergone refresher training on maintenance tasks in New Zealand.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For this exercise, CFC(NS) Pang was involved in the preparation of more than 10 SSPHs, which included servicing and maintaining of the guns.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The other two servicemen were also similarly qualified.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Gun Commander was in his eighth ICT and had undergone refresher training prior to his deployment in the exercise.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Regular technician has eight years of working experience on the SSPH and it was his sixth time participating as a technician in Exercise Thunder Warrior.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There are two levels of maintenance support – basic and higher.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Basic support is provided by the SSPH battalion's organic Forward Maintenance Platoon, made up of national servicemen.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: CFC(NS) Aloysius Pang was part of this Forward Maintenance Platoon.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If the repair works exceed the scope of the Forward Maintenance Platoon, more complex maintenance is requested from and performed by technicians in the higher maintenance echelon, and this is called the Forward Support Group, who are made up of Regulars.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, basic support made up of national servicemen, more complex maintenance made up of Regulars in the Forward Support Group.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In this particular incident, CFC(NS) Pang was first activated.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But as he was unable to resolve the fault, CFC(NS) Pang requested and received the help of Regular technicians from the Forward Support Group.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These are the three persons I referenced in the beginning of my Statement.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Second, the adequacy of safety protocols and whether the maintenance crew were familiar with them during this ICT.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: A number of Members of Parliament have asked for this, Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling, Prof Fatimah Lateef, Mr Darryl David, Miss Cheng Li Hui, Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong and Ms Joan Pereira.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I will focus on the relevant safety instructions during maintenance work, because this is the reason for the presence of these three people in the SSPH, and, in particular, when the gun is lowered.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There are safety procedures taught to all maintenance and SSPH operating crew.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The ME2 regular technician is overall in charge because he comes from the Forward Support Group and he is in charge of more complex repair works, so he is in charge.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Further, the safety instructions specify safe positions within the SSPH cabin for soldiers to occupy during the gun lowering, as well as safety precautions to be taken.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In operations or during maintenance, it is the Gun Commander who lowers the gun.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: From his Safe Position 1, indicated in the middle of this slide, the picture of the tank with the gun pointing forward or pointing up, the Gun Commander must first check to ensure that the gun barrel area is free from obstacles and that no persons are in the travel path of the barrel.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The other persons in the cabin are to occupy Safe Positions 2 or 3, on the left side and the right side respectively.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Gun Commander then gives the signal "clear away", "clear away" to warn the technicians about the barrel movement.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: He should visually check to ensure no persons are in the travel path of the barrel and all crew are in Safe Positions.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: After which, the Gun Commander should shout "standby" before moving the barrel.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In the event of any danger, there are also three emergency stop buttons in each of the safe positions inside the SSPH and they are indicated as the red buttons in each of the Safe Positions.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The warning is repeated for a variety of drills that the SSPH crew must undertake.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Next, I will show a video of this safety drill prescribed during the gun lowering – and it will be shown in actual speed, with your permission, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It takes about nine seconds for the gun to be lowered to the horizontal position for maintenance.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: All three persons who were in the cabin in this incident had been trained specifically on the SSPH and had conducted similar maintenance on it in the past.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: During this exercise, both CFC(NS) Pang and the Regular technician had conducted maintenance works on the guns daily.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Following the incident, the SAF's immediate task was to ensure that there was no systemic machine malfunction of the SSPH, which would otherwise have put maintenance crews at risk.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Third, was there a design flaw of the SSPH?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The SSPH was designed and developed to international military standards for System Safety and Human Factor Engineering.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Many other militaries operate tracked 155 millimetre (mm) guns with similar gun lowering mechanisms.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This includes the United States (US), South Korea and Germany.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The SSPH prototype platform underwent extensive trials and evaluations from year 2000 to 2002 before its introduction in 2003.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, it has been in operation for the last 15 years.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There has not been any reported injury of servicemen due to the gun lowering for maintenance, or operating in or firing of the SSPH.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I have stated the facts that MINDEF/SAF are aware of, in reply to Members' questions.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They include Mr Christopher de Souza, Mr Pritam Singh and Er Dr Lee Bee Wah.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We must now leave it to the independent five-member COI led by the State Court judge to determine the factors which led to the death of CFC(NS) Pang.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The COI has full access to material and witnesses to determine the facts for themselves.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For avoidance of doubt, let me reiterate that the COI need not take into account anything in my Statement in Parliament today.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Everything asked for by the COI will be released to them.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I do not foresee needing to withhold any information for security reasons.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In the meantime, the two other Servicemen deployed have been re-deployed from their operational roles.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We owe it to CFC(NS) Pang and his family, indeed to all Singaporeans, to get to the bottom of what happened, and make things right, to ensure the safety of the NS training system as a whole.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I ask that all of us respect these objective and impartial processes that are underway, to reserve our judgement and wait for the conclusions of the COI, which will be presented in Parliament subsequently.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As explained earlier in the House, the COI is enabled and governed by the SAF Act.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Its mandate is fact finding and not to determine culpability of individuals.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: To determine culpability, separate and independent from the COI, Police investigations are ongoing.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Thereafter, the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC) will decide if any persons should be prosecuted.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Internally, MINDEF will conduct its own investigations and may charge persons who breach military law in the Military Court, even if the AGC does not file criminal charges.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The COI of CFC Liu Kai will take into account findings from these various judicial processes before finalising its report.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As with all such exercises, a Regular trainer of Captain rank from the Active Unit Training Centre was assigned to evaluate the exercise troops.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The trainer used a Land Rover whose driver was CFC Liu, a Transport Operator.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This is the Bionix and the crew comprises four persons.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For this particular incident, an NSF who was in the position of the vehicle commander (Second Lieutenant), a rear guide when the vehicle reverses, he was the Third Sergeant NSF, the driver and the gunner who were both Corporals.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: On 2 November 2018, the trainer met the Bionix vehicle commander to understand their manoeuvre plan for the next day’s exercise.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The COI also found that the Land Rover that CFC Liu was driving was serviceable.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Land Rover has two cameras – one that records events in front of the vehicle, and the second that records events inside the cabin of the Land Rover.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The COI was able to piece together a detailed chronology from these camera recordings and statements from multiple witnesses.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I will bring Members through the events in detail by showing a series of graphics.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The exercise started on the morning of 3 November 2018 at 7.00 o'clock.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: CFC Liu and the trainer were in the Land Rover following their assigned Bionix.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: At around 9.58, the Bionix crew spotted several vehicles passing by at the junction ahead of it and stopped the Bionix, as ordered by the vehicle commander.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Responding to this, the Land Rover driven by CFC Liu also stopped.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The COI found that the trainer had instructed CFC Liu to move the Land Rover forward to overtake the Bionix.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Just as CFC Liu started to move forward slowly, shots were fired as part of the exercise.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: How well and quickly armour combat crews can extricate themselves when fired upon, can make a big difference as to whether they survive an enemy onslaught or are captured or destroyed.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The COI acknowledged the need for this type of training, even though it is high risk.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Bionix, as part of the prescribed drill, had to reverse so that its guns could continue to fire forward at the enemy.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As the driver of the Bionix is unable to see behind him or behind the vehicle, the rear guide directs the driver in reversing the vehicle.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Members would remember the picture I showed the Bionix with the driver in front – he can see forward.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is the rear guide who must guide him in reversing.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As the Bionix reversed, the Land Rover was initially not in its path.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The COI found that the Bionix had "drifted" in reversing and the driver made a slight steer to correct this drift.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This steer brought the Land Rover into the path of the Bionix.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The COI did not find any mechanical problems with the Bionix's steering equipment.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Almost immediately after the Bionix started reversing, the video recordings from the Land Rover's front facing camera show the Third Sergeant rear guide of the Bionix, quote, "gesturing at the Land Rover to move away and then pushing the mic of his helmet closer to his mouth".

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The COI found that the rear guide issued stop commands into the intercom of his helmet set when the Bionix started reversing and did so repeatedly.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The intercom of the helmet is the rear guide’s only means of communication with the other crew members in the Bionix.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The video recording of the interior of the Land Rover cabin showed the Captain trainer tapping CFC Liu and signalling him to reverse the Land Rover.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: From the beeping sounds, it also indicated that CFC Liu did engage the reverse gear.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Both the trainer and CFC Liu also shouted and gestured with their hands for the Bionix to stop and the trainer also attempted to reach for the handset of the radio set to communicate with the Bionix crew.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The trainer could extricate himself, but CFC Liu remained trapped.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The trainer notified the Conducting Officer of the exercise who immediately ordered the exercise to cease.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: A medic on board a nearby Bionix immediately tended to CFC Liu.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The SAF Emergency Ambulance Service (EAS), unit medical officer and Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) were activated and arrived on site.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: He was pronounced dead by the unit medical officer on site at around 1035 hours.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The cause of death, as determined by post-mortem, was traumatic asphyxia.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The COI noted that the rear guide had repeatedly given the order for the driver to stop reversing through the intercom via his helmet.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The COI noted that the intercom system was working earlier in the exercise.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The COI has asked for an independent technical assessment report on whether the intercom system was working properly all the time.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In parallel, Police investigations, too, are also focused on the communications between the Bionix crew and whether this was affected by the equipment.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This is, of course, an important point that needs to be resolved.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But we will have to await the outcome of the Police investigations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The COI made several findings in their report.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: First, the COI noted that ensuring the safety distance is the responsibility of the vehicle commander of the Land Rover.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In this case, the Land Rover ended up in a position that was less than the required safety distance from the Bionix.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Second, the reversing of the Bionix from the simulated enemy encounter brought the Land Rover into the path of the Bionix.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The COI found that a safety management plan was included as part of the exercise, and in line with standard practice.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The COI also found there was adequate deployment of medics and medical equipment as part of this plan for medical response.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I now share the ERPSS' written report on the COI findings, and it will be distributed to Members, with the Speaker's permission, and be made public subsequently.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: To summarise the report, they agreed with the COI's findings on the incident and proposed improvements that could be made to the safety management, emergency response system and combat vehicle safety, and the details are in the report.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Much of what the ERPSS commented, I have already outlined in my Ministerial Statement.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It will now be up to the AGC to decide if there are grounds to prosecute any person in the criminal Courts for the death of CFC Liu Kai.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If no criminal charges are filed, MINDEF will take disciplinary measures for lapses identified in this incident in our Military Court.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We will update Members and the public on these disciplinary measures.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In the meantime, the servicemen involved in this incident have been redeployed to non-operational roles.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: He served with pride and was remembered by his peers for his dedication and commitment.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We mourn the loss of this precious son.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And we hope that the measures SAF has put in place will prevent a similar incident in the future.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And these are questions that Members, including Mr Desmond Choo, have asked.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In response to the COI's findings and its own internal review, the following measures have or will be put in place by SAF.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, before the incident, there was one in front; now two more have been put in the rear of the Bionix for training vehicles.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This is to sound the alarm in the event of an intercom failure.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Army will study if these new features – the safety horns and the rear-view camera – ought to be incorporated for the operational vehicles as well.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: All heavy-wheeled vehicles, such as five-tonners, will also be progressively installed with rear-view cameras and mirrors to reduce blind spots.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This includes familiarisation with emergency measures and evacuation plans.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Fourth, more experienced Regulars have been added as trainers.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Sixth, vehicle and equipment serviceability will be improved based on the recommendations of the external panel.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In an exercise area, vehicles are used for a variety of administrative, safety and training purposes.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The current distance of 30 metres was prescribed after evaluation and tests and, in general, assessed to be adequate for safety and still allow supporting elements to be responsive to events on the ground.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But where vehicles have to reverse, such as in extrication drills, the Army has put in new measures to enhance safety.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: First, trainers will no longer travel in Land Rovers but will join exercise troops in the combat vehicles during high-risk training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Second, for all reversing manoeuvres, including extrication drills, the driver can only move the vehicle backwards with the explicit clearance of the rear guide.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These two measures, together with the extra emergency horn buttons, will enhance safety and still allow armour units to practise extrication drills.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Further, the Army will ensure that only essential vehicles are allowed into the exercise area to minimise the risk of accidents.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This move also responds to the ERPSS finding that while the safety policies and management systems of SAF are largely in place, there was a need for more compliance checks and ground level audits.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In line with this objective, SAF will undertake the following systemic measures.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Office will be headed by the SAF Inspector-General.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This dual function is synergistic as the COS-JS has an overview of all operations and, as Inspector-General, will have the authority to ensure that Safety First habits and processes are incorporated at all levels of training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: More safety officers will be deployed to assist individual units and supervise training activities.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There will be more safety audits of units by inspection teams in the Services and supervised by the IGO.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This is the right emphasis to prevent accidents.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In the past few weeks, the CDF reduced the tempo for every unit to review its processes and to emphasise to the troops a safety consciousness to protect themselves and their buddies.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Units that are on live operations, such as those protecting key installations, are not affected by this measure and will continue to be vigilant.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Basic types of training have resumed since 7 February.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Individual units will continue to be audited and will resume realistic training when safety processes are assessed to be in place.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Some Members – Mr Darryl David, Mr Chong Kee Hiong and Mr Leon Perera – have asked if external agencies review our system to detect root issues.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: ERPSS, which consists of prominent safety experts and professionals outside SAF, is tasked primarily with this mission.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The SAF's safety system is aligned to international frameworks and regulations, such as the Occupational Health and Safety System (OHSAS 18001) framework.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It comprises rules that mitigate safety risks in the conduct of all training; processes and training to build up competency of our servicemen and to make sure that the rules are properly applied; inspections and reporting mechanisms to ensure that the rules are followed; and consequences if they are not followed.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Quite a few Members – Prof Fatimah Lateef, Miss Cheng Li Hui, Ms Joan Pereira and Miss Cheryl Chan – have asked even if safety instructions are adequately in place, how do we ensure that national servicemen are familiar and safety conscious?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Also, whether SAF has taken into account the abrupt switch from civilian environment to military training where there are much larger and potentially dangerous equipment.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These are important issues that need to be factored into our safety systems.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: One suggestion has been to outsource all maintenance work with heavy vehicles or machinery.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Complex maintenance tasks that require specialised tools and equipment are already outsourced.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But we still need national servicemen technicians to be with their units to perform basic maintenance so that their equipment can function during operations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We do cater time for NSmen soldiers to adjust from their civilian settings.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Before any activity commences, a safety brief is held and inspections conducted to check that soldiers are in good physical state, and that vehicles and equipment are serviceable.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Soldiers must also complete an individual risk assessment checklist and raise safety concerns to their superiors for mitigation before any activity begins.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: NS training is conducted progressively, starting with refresher training for individual skills and proficiencies before any operations are conducted.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Prior to their deployment, further training, such as with a simulator, is conducted.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The IGO will review if further mitigating measures are needed to help NSmen adjust from civilian life to in-camp training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Members have asked, and this includes a question from Member Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, if we should punish safety lapses, even when they do not lead to injury.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: At the same time, we reward servicemen who demonstrate safe behaviour.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Units and individuals are recognised during the Service’s respective annual Safety Day.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If we are to achieve zero fatalities during NS training, we must have a strong safety culture in all our units and safety consciousness down to the last soldier.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Commanders and supervisors must lead by example to emphasise safety.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And all commanders already undergo safety training and must know that safety lapses will affect their performance review.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Safety Officers, who are former senior commanders, help ensure the safe conduct of training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Experienced Regular trainers partner the national servicemen commanders to design training and safety plans.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Soldiers must have a strong respect for safety rules, take care of one another and speak out on safety concerns.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Incentives and disincentives must be aligned to achieve the right safety outcomes.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Our safety system must weed out unsafe practices, even when they do not lead to accidents.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This was a point, I think, in the question of Member Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Individual soldiers are encouraged to report unsafe practices and risky behaviour to their superiors without fear of reprisal, or regardless of rank, to call for an immediate stop to training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We do not reward, nor should signal that we reward adventurous behaviour.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And this is in the Training Safety Regulations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is in chapter 1, section 2, paragraph 11: "Anyone who spots a safety breach or unsafe practice can call for an immediate stop to it, rectify when possible and report to the Conducting Officer.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Once notified, the Conducting Officer should verify the report and, when necessary, rectify the safety breach or unsafe practice.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Conducting Officer must update the Supervising Officer on the measures taken to rectify the safety breach or unsafe practice." Anyone who spots the safety breach; not only commanders, but anyone.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Ultimately, safety is both a command and individual responsibility and everyone needs to play their part because precious lives depend on it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is not true that we cannot train safely if we want to train realistically.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If we have a strong safety culture and safety systems, it will give soldiers greater confidence to train hard and realistically.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: SAF commanders are convinced that it can be done, and these measures I have outlined today will lead us to that goal of zero training fatalities.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It leaves a void that cannot be filled in the lives of family members and friends, and its impact is deep and far-reaching.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It will take much time for their grief to run its course.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Members Ms Anthea Ong and Mr Chong Kee Hiong have asked about assistance when a death occurs.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Within the SAF, dedicated grief counsellors are assigned to provide support to the serviceman’s family members in the aftermath of their loss.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For our soldiers, a team of psychologists, counsellors and psychiatrists are deployed to assist unit commanders and servicemen in their recovery from the stress in such incidents.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: MINDEF does take the families' request into consideration when deploying a deceased serviceman's immediate family members during their NS.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But I think the new safety measures we put into place after the devastating incidents of 2012 had an effect.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If we put our minds and efforts to achieve zero training fatalities, it can be achieved.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Four families have experienced much sorrow after their irreplaceable loss these past months.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As deep as the hurt, as great the loss, we must not forget why we suffer them.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: When the founding generation pledged themselves to build a strong SAF, they were fully conscious that a strong military is only possible with fully committed national servicemen drawn from every family in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They knew the costs and sacrifice that would be required.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Not only in resources that we invest in at every Budget, but much more precious would be the time, the sweat, the tears, even the lives of precious sons.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: On any given day within the SAF, thousands of national servicemen train hard, amid moving tonnes of steel, bullets, munitions and other explosives.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Because without national servicemen, we cannot have an SAF or the Home Team that can deter terrorists from attacking Changi Airport or Jurong or harming innocent civilians in shopping malls and crowded places.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Without national servicemen and the SAF, potential aggressors would not shy away from simply marching into and occupying today’s affluent Singapore, as Iraq did to Kuwait.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Without a strong defence, our air and shipping routes in and out of Singapore could easily be blocked – as Qatar now faces.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These are not imaginary security threats that our national servicemen train for, but real – they have happened elsewhere and can occur to Singapore, too.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We must never give up on NS that forms the backbone of our SAF for national defence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This imperative of NS and our national defence does not absolve or reduce the accountability of MINDEF and the SAF in any way, to ensure safe training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: On the contrary, it compels MINDEF and the SAF to do all that is humanly possible to prevent training deaths for national servicemen because precious sons have been entrusted to us by their families.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Even as we honour those who died in service of our country, we must soldier on, to build a strong defence, to protect Singapore and to protect every national serviceman during training.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With the time that has passed since the incident and the timeout was originally called for, I do hope that SAF and the commanders will also observe as much safety precautions as possible as men catch up on the training that they have missed out during this period of time.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The second question is with regard to further assuring Singaporean parents.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Fellow residents in my constituency knew him well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Over the course of the last few weeks, as I visited families in their flats as we held gatherings, many parents have come up to me and asked about safety, about reassurances for their children.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But what I am heartened by is that none of the parents that have spoken to me have ever said we should do away with NS.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, how do we reassure them that safety is paramount, that their children will be taken care of?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I was previously with the Transport Section of the 328th Battalion Singapore Combat Engineers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I looked after the five-tonners as well as other transport equipment.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: How different is this timeout from previous timeouts?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You must start on the basis that there might be something wrong and look for that factor, whatever that factor is, and that is just a precaution.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, there is not as if after a certain period, behaviours will automatically correct.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But as Members can well imagine, SAF runs platforms of various generations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In fact, the most recent generations, the Terrexes, even our Leopard tanks, have rear-view cameras.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But you inherit a long tail and the Bionix was in operation since, I think, the 1990s.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, I would say, in principle, yes, but there are other considerations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But, in principle, that is what we want to do.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And, certainly, as I said, for those that need to reverse, that are reversing, we will put in not only rear-view cameras but mirrors to reduce blind spots.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There was another question of reassurance of parents.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: How do you reassure parents that their sons will be safe?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And I am glad what the Member Mr Alex Yam has said, that no parent has come to him to say they want to do away with NS.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The parents want to know that you are doing your level best and that you will pay attention.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But let me give Members another perspective as well in these two incidents and a number of incidents that I shared in this House.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I shared with Members the incident of Gavin Chan who was training overseas as well when his Bionix overturned.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And I gave Members the findings of the COI.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: When asked by his crew to switch on the headlights, he said, "We should not do it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It would give our position away to the enemy".

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In the case of Dave Lee, the heatstroke, he pushed himself beyond what he was able.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In this case, Liu Kai, they wanted to be realistic, extrication drills.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have come very far when national servicemen say, "I want to train as realistically as I can".

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: What if we had the reverse situation where everyone attends training but nobody trains?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think we have to take what is good in our system and respond practically.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The results must be the ultimate comfort for parents.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We will do as much as we can practically each time our COIs tell us there is a lapse or a weakness that needs to be addressed.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But I need at every level a safety consciousness, a safety culture.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And I tell Members that it does not come overnight and may not come even after many years, to raise the level of safety culture.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I had been the Minister for Manpower, and Members will remember the particular period, the Nicoll Highway collapse, the Fusionopolis incident, the COIs that we had.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In order to strengthen our system, we went overseas to the Nordic countries, to some European countries, which have higher standards than us.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They told me a very interesting example of a particular bridge that was built by two Nordic countries.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I will not name them because there are implications which will be explained once I have shared.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Two Nordic countries building a bridge to connect the two.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Same specifications, they will meet in the middle.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: One country had half the number of deaths and injuries of the other country.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If you think it is unsafe for your buddies, for yourself, raise it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If you think that somebody is pushing beyond his means to physical harm, do so.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That way, we maintain realistic training and give comfort to our parents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can I ask the Minister at what level would this be?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would it be at the battalion level, the brigade or the division, formation level?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Related to this, I note that the NS training deaths in recent years have involved different vocations, different formation and command.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think in some of these cases where disciplinary actions have been taken, they were taken against junior or mid-level commanders.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I say this, bearing in mind some examples from overseas.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 2013, a Taiwanese conscript died after being physically punished by his superiors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Four officers were charged and the Defence Minister was also quick to take responsibility.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The reason given was that there was a loss of confidence in his ability to command.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the same time, while each of these four incidents is unique, they cannot be viewed in isolation – that was the reason given.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Also, the US Navy went on to say that there will be a deliberate reset of all the ships, focus on navigation, mechanical systems and bridge resource management.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As I have said, even those that do not lead to accidents will affect their performance review.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We want to be careful that we do what we think works and makes a difference.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And if you think that that improves the system, push for it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But let us deal with the issue on the ground.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I have presented the facts as much as I can.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have had independent reviews, people outside SAF and MINDEF all looking into the problem.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And if they decide that a change of the most senior leadership makes a difference, well, it is up to them to recommend.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But, for MINDEF and SAF, we want to deal with day-to-day issues, aligning our incentives and disincentives so we get the whole system moving and making sure that the effect is felt on the ground, rather than posturing or politicking.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As a serving NSman, I think incidents like this move us very strongly because we know it could be us or any other people serving with us.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In relation to this, I have two questions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In any organisation like the army, we know the work we do is inherently risky and, if any human error is made, incidents can happen.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think the Minister mentioned as Minister for Manpower, he looked at other countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Are there any armies we can learn from?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The second question is: if this incident is the result of, say, human error rather than systemic lapses, is there a need to halt training across the whole system?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: My concern, of course, is the message we may send to other parties who would be looking at us to see whether the Singapore army is able to deal with adversity.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Most serving NSmen I have spoken to remain ready to serve and ready to go forward.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have looked at figures to see what injury and fatality rates for other militaries are.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Of course, we want to benchmark and make sure that we are somewhere there.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But that is difficult because you cannot compare like and like.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Systems with conscript systems, Taiwan and South Korea, their data is shared in different ways.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They may have different terrain and so on and so forth.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have to ask ourselves, where is our system at?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And when we ask these questions, remember as the Member said, so many of us here have or are serving NS.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We know what it is about and some of you even blog your experiences when you go to NS.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is not divorced from reality where there is one group doing NS and another group just commenting on it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The very people who comment are the ones who do it every year when you go in and you know what the reality is.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If you think that the system has degraded to a point, point out where it is and we will fix it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But if we are experiencing injuries and deaths as a result – as the Member said, human error – then neither should we punish indiscriminately even those who are not involved nor degrade what has taken years for us to achieve.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That does not bring anyone any comfort or positive results.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Deal with the issue, strengthen the system bit by bit, and it will take years.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You know how it is with some commercial companies.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Before every board meeting, they repeat the same thing over and over again – the safety instructions, they tell you where the exits are.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And I was told that even in some countries, the safety officer saw some chap walking up the stairs not using the stair rail and says, "This is a safety breach – you should use the stair rail because you can fall." You say it may be overboard, but there is a meaning to it, I think.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You need to have proper instructions, and each time something happens, we must be open, we will review it, get independent parties to look at it, and then strengthen it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Do we want a system where everyone is afraid?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You walk into a room, and everyone is frightened that if anything happens, his head will be chopped, more heads will be chopped, up, down.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I have dealt with many organisations, both in my private life and in Government.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I noticed that the best organisations run not ones which are on tenterhooks, fearful of reprisals so that they dare not do anything, and not ones that are slack.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In fact, a slightly busy outfit is the best outfit.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You go into any organisation, you want people who are professional, who know what they do, who are conscious, who are not out just to punish unfairly, but to say how do I make this system better because it will take time, it will take effort, and it will take the part of everybody in their organisation to do so.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Indeed, we must strive to marry safety and creating a real operational environment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These retired or near-to-retirement SAF officers and Specialists have a wealth of experience to share; this could be a body separate from IGO.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That is exactly one of the resources that we looked upon.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, because of this, we have redeployed, put safety as a priority.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But we will also look for other avenues where we can put more experience on the ground to help our national servicemen as well as young officers build up the training and safety capabilities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My first pertains to the non-operational responsibilities on NSmen and NSFs, such as National Day Parades (NDPs) and Army Half Marathon.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some would be of the view that some aspects of organising such events could be undertaken by the private sector.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that extent, is MINDEF, as part of this safety review, looking into the time NSFs and NSmen have, to focus on training, maintenance and other operational responsibilities?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second one pertains to the handout that the Minister gave.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This was the External Review Panel's report on the COI's preliminary findings on the death of CFC Liu Kai.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister share why CFC Liu Kai was not evacuated promptly even though it does state earlier in the report that even if he could have been evacuated, he probably still would have demised from his injuries.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I agree with the Member that we want to be careful as we are moving in this safety journey to allow time for units to focus on safety and, if there are administrative aspects that deter them from it, then we should be prepared to relook.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: CDF, the Commanders, the Commanding Officers (COs) of the units must themselves come to and decide which is the tempo, and the Member is quite right.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I will leave it to them to announce what they are not going to do, so that it gives them enough bandwidth to focus on safety.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For CFC Liu Kai's extrication, Members will understand why I have not gone into details.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Just now, the Minister mentioned that anybody can stop training if they find that it is not safe.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Is there a hotline or is there a whistleblower hotline?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How to assure them that they will not be dealt with unfairly later on if they were to report or being "tekan"?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: On the ground, usually in activities, you have a safety officer and a conducting officer.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But even the CO of the activity who is supervising and the other conducting officers, if you bring it up to them, we want to have a culture where the person can assess the safety and risks.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The message is very clear to the units after this Statement.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But if it needs to be clearer because of the reiteration, then remember that unsafe practices will not be tolerated.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I met a family of a deceased soldier about two years ago and his mother told me it is hard for the pain to go away.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In fact, she told me, it will never go away.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a mother, I felt for her and I can understand fully her pain.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I know the Minister highlighted earlier about the support through grief counsellors given to the platoon mates and to the families of the deceased soldiers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I would like to know if such emotional and psychological support is sufficient and if, indeed, more can be done to provide such support to the families.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: All of us can imagine how difficult it is for any parent and mothers to have to lose their sons.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And all we can do is to pray that there will be some comfort.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I have already shared how we provide relief by grief counsellors.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But even our efforts need to be very sensitive.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Not all families can accept it at the time.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But we should always just be there to offer the help and be consistently there if it is needed.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The first one is when can we expect the findings of the COI on CFC (NS) Pang's case, if there is an indication as to when the findings will be released?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The second is, we all know, there cannot be total safety without psychosocial safety.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister share a little bit of the elements within this safety culture we are building that relates to the psychosocial safety climate, please?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, they take as much time as they need, and I have no control over how fast or how quickly they want to conclude it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The psychosocial aspect is incredibly important, and we are not dealing with something which is esoteric.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The need for safety, whether it is construction, heavy machinery, and the same challenges we face in the workplace also apply to both military and civilian settings.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, it is a science and there are experts at it; and there are benchmarks.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As I have said, this is intangible of safety culture.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And in these conversations like I had, like many Members had over this Chinese New Year period when we talked about why this is happening, and there is always somewhat a tendency to say, "Well, one generation is different from the other." In the Merdeka Generation, in the Pioneer Generation, it is more of aware of risks, because when we grew up, when we crossed roads, it was always a run or very hazardous.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But a newer generation lives in a more structured environment.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I do not know what the truth is.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We will just have to deal with it and keep strengthening and keep tightening where we feel that it has to be and continue to move it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And if more people buy into this safety culture, I think it will help.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is very clear this is a Command responsibility.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Also, being a Director of Quality, Clinical Service and Patient Safety in Emergency Medicine and Trauma, so, that really has got a synergy between the two.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The fact that the Minister mentioned that the incorporation of safety culture practices into the whole organisation is welcomed.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But more than that, looking at the examples given by the Minister and the whole description, it is actually about human factors – human factors and human errors.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: So, there are people who study human factors, human factor science, human factor analysis and perhaps, this is one area of focus, not just after an incident happens but also perhaps as a preventive measure to get human factor specialists to actually study some of the more high-risk activities.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Probably, you will not be able to study all the activities that go on in the SAF, just as we cannot do it in medicine.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But perhaps the more high-risk activities that people are going to be involved in, and especially, compared to medicine, you are involved with more heavy machinery and equipment.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: So, how do we use human factor specialists to help us with this?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Member has raised a very important, relevant point and it is incorporated.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: All our services do it, to some extent.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But the Army is a much larger machinery and many tens of thousands of people running around.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But we have got to get that into our system at every level.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And it will be up to commanders, and they are going to give it their all because they know this is their moral responsibility, this is their professional accountability, and this is something that we must get right.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What difference, how much more different and how much effective can it be?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I know some servicemen, for some reasons, may not want to report some of these incidents because of unit cohesion and other matters as well.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, that will be part of the menu of things that we will have to ramp up.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But we want to make sure that it is more accessible and the message gets through.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Well, when the Inspector-General, who is the Chief of Staff-Joint Staff (COS-JS), calls you, you listen, and you better listen.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What is known about the reasons why this instruction was given?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Second, was CFC Liu familiar with these aspects?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As I have said, extrication drills are part and parcel of the exercise.
